functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Long fascicles like its neighbor brachioradialis; most radial of the wrist extensors.
functional_compartments.source: Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

motor_endplate_zones.method: cadaveric dissection -- radial-nerve motor branch entry point (motor point) location, not a Sihler's-stain arborization density map
motor_endplate_zones.notes: In all 30 dissected limbs (100%), the nerve branch to ECRL entered the muscle within its proximal third; the branch itself averaged 2.9 +/- 1.0 motor sub-points and 3.2 +/- 1.0 cm in length. Motor point (nerve entry) is typically close to, but not identical with, the point of densest intramuscular arborization -- treat this range as a proximal-third targeting zone rather than a fine-grained endplate band.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Caetano EB, Vieira LA, Sabongi Neto JJ, Caetano MBF, Picin CP, Silva Junior LCN, 'Anatomical Study of the Motor Branches of the Radial Nerve in the Forearm', Rev Bras Ortop (Sao Paulo) 55(6):764-770 (2020), doi:10.1055/s-0040-1713403 (https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0040-1713403) -- 30 limbs from 15 adult cadavers -- retrieved via PubMed

trigger_points.location_description: Muscle belly about 3-5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, radial to extensor carpi radialis brevis and just dorsal to brachioradialis.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Lateral epicondyle region and the radial dorsal wrist over the anatomical snuffbox and the bases of the 1st-2nd metacarpals; painful weak grip is the characteristic complaint.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Repetitive gripping with wrist extension (racquet backhand, mouse and keyboard work, scrubbing, hand-shaking), lifting with a pronated forearm; commonly co-exists with brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis brevis, supinator and extensor digitorum trigger points.
trigger_points.notes: Active ECRL trigger points reproduced the presenting pain in 12 of 20 patients with lateral epicondylalgia (Fernandez-Carnero et al. 2007). Non-myofascial differential: intersection syndrome, De Quervain's disease, radial sensory neuritis, STT and basal-joint arthritis, scaphoid pathology, dorsal wrist ganglion, scapholunate injury, C6 radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 34; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 34, pp. 329-342 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: ECRL extends and radially deviates the wrist; with ECRB it is the wrist stabiliser that keeps the finger flexors at an efficient length during grip, which is why gripping loads the lateral epicondylar origins. Its line of pull anterior to the elbow axis gives it a weak elbow-flexion moment, largest with the forearm pronated or neutral. In the lateral-epicondylalgia model it is the muscle that compresses ECRB against the capitellar edge in extension. It is a common tendon-transfer donor (to FDP or FPL).
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None named at the elbow; an adventitial bursa may form at the APL/EPB crossing (intersection syndrome). Adjacent structures and relations: Radial nerve and its division deep and medial at the elbow; superficial radial nerve emerging between its tendon and brachioradialis distally; ECRB immediately deep and posterior; the radial collateral ligament complex deep to its origin.

trigger_points.location: Proximal muscle belly, a few centimetres distal to the lateral epicondyle along the supracondylar ridge, palpated against brachioradialis.
trigger_points.referred_pain: lateral epicondyle and lateral elbow, and to the dorsal-radial hand and wrist in the region of the anatomical snuffbox.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: "Tennis elbow", weak painful grip, painful handshake, dorsal-radial wrist pain resembling de Quervain tenosynovitis or intersection syndrome. In lateral epicondylalgia patients ECRL TrPs reproduced the presenting pain in 70% (Fernández-Carnero 2007). Entrapment: None attributed to ECRL TrPs; its tendon forms one wall of the Wartenberg compression site for the superficial radial nerve. Associated TrPs: Brachioradialis, ECRB, supinator, extensor digitorum, triceps.

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO this territory from elsewhere
clinical.notes: Kocher and Kaplan lateral approaches pass anterior to or through the ECRL–ECRB interval; the PIN is protected by pronation. Loss of ECRL in radial nerve palsy above the elbow removes wrist extension; PT-to-ECRB transfer is the standard replacement.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.

tests.name: Cozen's test
tests.performance: Elbow stabilised, forearm pronated, fist clenched; resisted wrist extension with radial deviation
tests.accuracy: Sensitivity 91% in a single small study; specificity not established (Karanasios 2022 review)
tests.source: Karanasios S, Korakakis V, Moutzouri M, Drakonaki E, Koci K, Pantazopoulou V, et al. Diagnostic accuracy of examination tests for lateral elbow tendinopathy (LET): a systematic review. J Hand Ther. 2022;35(4):541–551.

tests.name: Grip-strength difference / pain-free grip
tests.performance: Dynamometry with the elbow extended vs flexed; a 5–10% drop with extension is the criterion
tests.positive_finding: Reduced grip with the elbow extended
tests.source: Karanasios S, Korakakis V, Moutzouri M, Drakonaki E, Koci K, Pantazopoulou V, et al. Diagnostic accuracy of examination tests for lateral elbow tendinopathy (LET): a systematic review. J Hand Ther. 2022;35(4):541–551.

tests.name: Chair and coffee-cup tests
tests.performance: Lifting a chair or a full cup with a pronated grip
tests.source: Zwerus EL, Somford MP, Maissan F, Heisen J, Eygendaal D, van den Bekerom MPJ. Physical examination of the elbow, what is the evidence? A systematic literature review. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(19):1253–1260.

tests.name: Trigger-point examination
tests.performance: Palpation of taut bands in brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB, ED and supinator
tests.positive_finding: Reproduction of the presenting lateral elbow pain
tests.accuracy: Referred pain reproduced the presenting pain in 50–70% of patients with lateral epicondylalgia (Fernández-Carnero 2007)
tests.source: Fernández-Carnero J, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, de la Llave-Rincón AI, Ge HY, Arendt-Nielsen L. Prevalence of and referred pain from myofascial trigger points in the forearm muscles in patients with lateral epicondylalgia. Clin J Pain. 2007;23(4):353–360.

clinical.tests_caveat: Values are taken from the cited primary studies. Most series are small and reference standards differ (surgery, arthroscopy, electrodiagnostics), so treat the numbers as indicative. The systematic review of Zwerus et al. (2018) found 24 described elbow tests, only 14 with any accuracy data, and concluded that no single test can rule an elbow diagnosis in or out on its own. Where no accuracy data exist, this is stated rather than estimated.

(2019) for trigger-point (TrP) locations and referred-pain patterns; Green's Operative Hand Surgery 8th ed. (2022) [4], Neumann (2017) [5], Kendall (2005) [6] and Kapandji (2019) [7] for kinesiology, Netter (2023) [54] for topographic cross-checking; and peer-reviewed primary literature for biomechanics, variants and clinical entities. Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Radial deviation: the largest radial-deviation moment arm of the extensors (about 22 mm), with a moderate extension moment arm (about 11 mm) [10, 12]. Minor: Wrist extension; weak elbow flexion (especially with the forearm pronated) [1, 6]. Strength: PCSA about 1.5 cm², smaller than ECRB or ECU, with long fibres and large excursion; its stiff tendon (about 1.8% strain at maximal load) suits position control [8, 11, 12]. Extensor torque varies with wrist angle because extensor moment arms change through the range [10]. Carpal stability: Carpal supinator, protective for the scapholunate joint and most efficient with the forearm pronated; first-phase motor of the dart-throwing motion together with APL [14, 16, 19]. Importance: Wrist stabilizer during grip (synergist to the finger flexors); frequent transfer donor (ECRL to FDP in spastic hands and tetraplegia, ECRL to ECU for wrist rebalancing) because ECRB alone can extend the wrist [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: 2nd compartment synovial sheath from about 2 cm proximal to the retinaculum toward the insertion. A small bursa between the ECRL/ECRB tendons and the 2nd–3rd metacarpal bases is described in the carpal-boss literature [grade C]. Relations: Superficial branch of the radial nerve emerges between brachioradialis and ECRL tendons in the distal third of the forearm (Wartenberg's compression site) [36]; radial artery lies palmar to it in the snuffbox. Coupled structures: Superficial radial nerve, APL/EPB bellies, EPL tendon, 2nd carpometacarpal joint (carpal boss), scapholunate ligament (via carpal supination) [14, 35, 36].

trigger_points.location: Muscle belly about 3–5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, radial to ECRB and just dorsal to brachioradialis (chapter 34, "Pseudo tennis elbow") [2, 3].
trigger_points.referred_pain: Lateral epicondyle region and the radial dorsal wrist over the anatomical snuffbox and the bases of the 1st–2nd metacarpals; painful weak grip is the characteristic complaint [2, 3].
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Repetitive gripping with wrist extension (racquet backhand, mouse and keyboard work, scrubbing, hand-shaking), lifting with a pronated forearm; commonly co-exists with brachioradialis, ECRB, supinator and EDC trigger points [3, 34].

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred into ECRL territory (radial dorsal wrist)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: Intersection syndrome, De Quervain's disease, radial sensory neuritis, STT and basal-joint arthritis, scaphoid pathology, dorsal wrist ganglion, scapholunate injury, C6 radiculopathy.
clinical.notes: Intersection syndrome is a peritendinitis where the APL and EPB bellies cross ECRL/ECRB (rowers, weightlifters, racquet sports); pain and crepitus are felt 4–8 cm proximal to the wrist [35]. Distal intersection with EPL is the rarer counterpart. Wartenberg's syndrome is compression of the superficial radial nerve between the brachioradialis and ECRL tendons in pronation [36]. ECRL contributes less than ECRB to lateral epicondylalgia but harbours active trigger points in most such patients (12 of 20) [34]. A carpal boss forms at the ECRL/ECRB insertions.
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
